name: Probate
round: Round V4 · sent 11 Sep 2026 by Vadim, your BA · replaces V3
description: What happens to an investor’s shares and money when they die. You have answered every question we asked; three narrow follow-ups are left, and only question 1 holds up a screen.
problem: When a shareholder dies, the platform has no way to hold their shares. Interest keeps being paid out to the dead person’s account, and the only fix is a manual correction afterwards.
solution: Death is recorded once on the person, and every holding it affects pauses together. Money stops leaving while interest keeps accruing. When the executor brings the grant of probate, one release pays out everything that was withheld.

design.label: What this feature is
design.more_label: The rest of the design, and where it has got to
design.summary:
When a shareholder dies, money stops leaving their holdings until the executor produces the grant of probate — and then one release pays out everything that was withheld. Death is recorded once on the person, not on each certificate, so every holding that death affects pauses together.

Seven screens are drawn and thirty-four acceptance criteria are written. The three questions below are the only things still open.
design.detail:
The design deliberately keeps the executor out of the platform. There is no executor login: an Admin keys the split from the executor’s written instruction, and that instruction is filed alongside the grant of probate, so the record shows what was keyed, by whom, and against what.

Interest keeps accruing through the hold. A joint holding only pauses once every holder has died — where rights of survivorship apply the surviving holder takes the shares directly and no hold should fire at all.

screens.cap: The release screen. Question 1 is about this form: it shows the transferee named at onboarding, and the executor's instruction may name four different people.
What a relative sees using the dead person's credentials — everything readable, nothing changeable, and no notice that a hold is on. Question 2 is about this screen.
After release. No reinvestments and no new shares, ever. Question 3 asks who empties the wallet once the last certificate matures.

decisions.detail: A deceased investor never becomes an ordinary one again.

The investor side shows no probate message

decisions.title: An estate may redeem early, and the fee still applies
decisions.detail: After release, shares stay active to maturity, only an Admin can trigger early redemption, and there are no reinvestments or new shares.

Probate works on any investor, even one with an unfinished profile
decisions.detail: Their money goes to a wallet and is released the same way.

decisions.title: Applications caught part-way through are cancelled
decisions.detail: The money goes back to the estate, into a wallet. One rule for all four states.

decisions.detail: The grant still gates the release. Money can go to a bank account, other investors' wallets, or both, through the existing wallet-transfer flow.

decisions.title: Death is recorded once on the investor, and every holding pauses together

questions.section: A — The one that holds a screen up
questions.title: Whose list of heirs wins — the one they chose at sign-up, or the grant of probate?
questions.meta: Decides — what the release screen does when the two disagree
questions.body:
Your answer on 11 September settled who types the split in: an Admin, working from the executor's written instruction. This is the thing sitting underneath it.

When an investor signs up they name a single transferee — one person, “in the event of death”. We already hold that on the record and the release screen shows it. A grant of probate can name several heirs in different shares, and it does not have to agree with a nomination made years earlier.

So when the screen shows one name and the executor's instruction says four people at 25% each, which does the Admin follow?
questions.snag: Our reading is that the grant wins — it is the legal instrument and it is current, where the nomination is a preference recorded years before. But we do not want to build that in quietly. The nomination is a field the investor filled in deliberately, it will still be on the screen, and an Admin who sees two answers and no rule will pick one.
questions.note: If the grant always decides, is there still a reason to collect the nominated transferee at sign-up?

options.t: The grant of probate wins, always
options.d: Our suggestion. The nomination stays on screen for context but never decides anything, and we label it so an Admin cannot mistake it for an instruction.

options.t: Follow the nomination when it agrees with the grant, flag it when it does not
options.d: Feels safer, but the system cannot do that comparison reliably — a name match is not proof, and a part-match needs a human anyway. In practice it becomes the option above with extra steps.

options.t: Stop showing the nomination on the release screen at all
options.d: Cleanest screen and no ambiguity, but you lose a fact the investor recorded on purpose, and it may still matter in cases where no grant has been produced yet.
Describe it in the box below.

questions.title: Does anyone outside this project need to see the read-only login decision?
questions.meta: Decides — whether this is recorded beyond a design document
questions.body:
Nothing here is blocked and we are not asking you to change your answer. We are asking where it should be written down.

You chose to leave a dead person's login open but read-only. That is in the spec and it is buildable as it stands.

The part that came back blank was the other half: does compliance already know that relatives use a dead person's credentials? Read-only stops them changing anything, but they can still read statements, holdings and personal details belonging to someone who has died. That is a data-protection matter rather than a probate one, which is why we would rather ask than assume.
questions.snag: Why we are asking at all. If this is known and accepted, one sentence from you puts it on the record as a decision rather than leaving it looking like something nobody noticed. If it is not known, it is better found now than during an audit.
questions.note: Is this worth a line in the privacy policy or the investor agreement rather than only our spec?

options.t: It is known and accepted — record it and move on
options.d: Our suggestion if that is the case. We note it in the spec as a deliberate decision with your name against it, and build the read-only rule as answered. Nothing else changes.

options.t: Raise it with compliance before we build the rule
options.d: We hold the read-only behaviour until you come back. Everything else in probate carries on — this is the only piece that would wait.

options.t: Change the answer — disable the login after all
options.d: Small to swap. Read-only becomes a hard block, and the estate is served by an Admin from the moment death is recorded.
Describe it in the box below.

questions.section: C — The last of the money
questions.title: Who empties the estate's wallet, and is an estate ever formally finished?
questions.meta: Decides — whether anything reminds us the money is there
questions.body:
You said the wallet must be emptied at the end rather than left to sit. Agreed, and written down. What is not settled is who notices.

When the last certificate matures, the principal lands in the estate's wallet. Today nothing tells anyone it is there — and by then the estate may have been quiet for a year.

There is also no state on the record that says an estate is finished. That means nobody can answer “which estates are still holding money?” without going through them one at a time.
questions.note: Is there a legal point at which an estate is wound up that we should be recording against the investor?

options.t: The system flags it, an Admin pays it out
options.d: Our suggestion. A deceased investor with a wallet balance and no live certificates appears on a list, and an Admin clears it to the bank account already captured at release. Small to build, and it answers the reporting question at the same time.

options.t: An Admin does it when they notice
options.d: Nothing to build. It relies on someone remembering months after the estate went quiet, which is exactly how dormant balances happen.

options.t: Add a proper "estate closed" step that pays out and locks the record
options.d: Most to build, but you get a real answer to whether an estate is done, and a report of the ones that are not.
Describe it in the box below.
